newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Fugitive lawmaker puts Philippine justice on trial.
newsitem.headline: Fugitive lawmaker puts Philippine justice on trial.

text.p: In a country where the long arm of the law is notoriously short, a Philippine congressman evading arrest on charges of having sex with an 11-year-old girl has put the entire justice system on trial, political analysts said.

A nationwide, 18-day manhunt that began with stakeouts around House of Representatives member Romeo Jalosjos's apartments in Manila and spread last week to Indonesia has failed to produce any trace of the lawmaker belonging to President Fidel Ramos's ruling coalition in Congress.
"It just strengthens mistrust in the judicial system," said Teresita Ang See, head of the citizens anti-crime watchdog group Movement for the Restoration of Peace and Order.
"People say, 'what can you expect'," See said, referring to perceptions often voiced among Filipinos that the powerful and the rich are beyond the reach of the law.

The perceptions have endured despite the jailing in recent years of another ruling party congressman for arms smuggling, a town mayor for rape and murder, a feared police colonel for kidnapping and a popular movie actor for illegal possession of firearms.
"Even if there have been convictions, those were exceptions that only prove the rule," human rights lawyer Rene Saguisag said.
A judge ordered the 56-year-old Jalosjos arrested on December 26 after the schoolgirl told police the congressman had sex with her several times in his apartment last year.
She said he gave her amounts of up to 10,000 pesos ($385) each time. Prosecutors said the girl's father brought her to the politician. The father faces a separate charge of exploitation.
Jalosjos has denied having met the girl and said the charges are "a fairy tale".

Ramos ordered a full-scale manhunt for the congressman after he evaded arrest for more than a week, despite a judge issuing warrants for his detention. Many newspapers reported at the time that Jalosjos was known to be in Manila.
Last week, police said they had received a tip-off that Jalosjos had taken a boat to Indonesia and the Foreign Office has sought Jakarta's help.
Lawyers blame the decline of public confidence in the justice system on the late president Ferdinand Marcos.
After declaring martial law in 1972, Marcos removed many judges and prosecutors and even appointed former law school classmates to the Supreme Court, wrecking the judiciary's independence, they said.
"We have not recovered from the trauma," Saguisag said. "...justice is for sale," he said.

"The system does tend to favour those who are powerful and have money," analyst and columnist Nelson Navarro said. "In a country where there is corruption, the system favours the one who has the resources," he told Reuters.
Navarro added, however, that the Philippines' unfettered press was a powerful watchdog against abuses.
"The power of public opinion, the power of media tips the scale.

"This is definitely a test case, a test between the power of a politician and of money versus an enraged citizenry and media. Those in the establishment are finding to their grief that they are not as invulnerable as they used to be."

One of those who does not believe justice cuts equally between the rich and the poor is tourist guide Silvino Salarza. Convicted of raping a British actress on a tourist island, he is one of 282 people on death row at the national penitentiary.
"When they hang a rich man, that's the time I will believe in justice," he told Reuters during an interview in his prison cell two weeks ago.
